content.title: About
content.content: Cashews are the edible seeds of the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), native to tropical regions of South America and now cultivated in Asia, Africa and the Caribbean. They have a mild, buttery‑sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. Cashews are eaten raw, roasted, or baked, and are used in sauces, pastes, desserts, and plant‑based milks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cashew nut hangs from the bottom of a fleshy fruit called the cashew apple, which is also edible.
Unsalted cashews are often sold as whole nuts, but they are sometimes lightly roasted to enhance flavor.
Cashews are a rich source of copper, an essential mineral for iron metabolism and connective tissue formation.
In India, cashews are a key ingredient in traditional sweets such as kaju katli and kaju barfi.
Unlike many other nuts, cashews have a thin skin that is easy to digest.

items.title: High in copper
items.content: Copper in cashews supports red blood cell formation and immune function.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: The majority of fat in cashews is monounsaturated, which can help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while phosphorus is important for bone health.

items.title: Provides plant protein and fiber
items.content: Cashews supply a good blend of amino acids and dietary fiber, promoting satiety and digestive health.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: They contain tocopherols and phenolic compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Cashews can trigger allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because they are calorie‑dense, portion control is recommended.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: People prone to kidney stones may need to limit cashew intake due to oxalates.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: Whole cashews are not suitable for children under 4 years old.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cashews can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, oatmeal, yogurt, used in sauces, pastes (cashew butter), baked goods, or made into plant‑based milk. Soaking softens them and makes skin removal easier. Unsalted cashews are a wholesome option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cashews in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Graham crackers are dry baked biscuits made from whole‑wheat flour, sugar, honey and vegetable oil. They have a light sweet note, a crisp texture and are often used in desserts such as cheesecakes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Originally developed in the United States at the end of the 19th century as a healthier alternative to sweet cookies.
The name comes from the “Graham” brand, founded by Sylvester Graham, who promoted whole‑grain foods.
They are a key component of the classic American treat “s’mores” – layered with melted chocolate and toasted marshmallows.
Traditional recipes use whole‑wheat flour, retaining bran and germ.
Graham crackers can be found in both sweet and mildly salty versions, depending on the recipe.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Graham crackers supply iron, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many sweet cookies, they contain a modest amount of fat.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains deliver B1, B3 and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index
items.content: The whole‑grain base leads to a steadier rise in blood sugar than refined white bread.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with gluten intolerance or wheat allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some varieties contain added sugar, which may be a concern for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Savory versions can be relatively high in salt, which should be considered in hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Graham crackers can be enjoyed as a snack, used as a base for desserts (cheesecake, s’mores), crumbled into yogurt, mixed with dried fruit, or employed as a coating for frying.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, refrigerate to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese pizza is a popular fast‑food and restaurant dish consisting of a crust topped with tomato sauce and a generous layer of melted cheese. Mozzarella is most common, but cheddar, parmesan, or a blend of cheeses are often used.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cheese pizza was made in Naples in the 19th century.
The most popular crust type for cheese pizza is thin crust, though deep‑dish is common in the United States.
More than 30 varieties of cheese can be used, each giving a distinct flavor and texture.
In Japan, cheese pizza is frequently garnished with seaweed and mayonnaise.
In 2012, over 3 billion servings of cheese pizza were sold in the United States.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese provides a good amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: The cheese layer supplies complete animal protein that supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory compounds
items.content: Certain cheeses (e.g., mozzarella) contain conjugated linoleic acid, which may help reduce inflammation.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Hard cheeses such as parmesan can contain live cultures that support gut microbiota.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese is often salty, and excessive intake can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Large portions of cheese pizza can increase saturated fat consumption, which may affect heart health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after eating regular cheese pizza.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to casein, a protein found in cheese.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese pizza is typically eaten hot, sliced into wedges. Additional toppings such as ham, vegetables, or herbs can be added. For a lighter option, choose whole‑grain crust and reduce the amount of cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover pizza in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore a crisp crust. Pizza can be frozen for up to 2 months if wrapped tightly in plastic film.

content.title: About
content.content: Veal scallopini are thinly pounded pieces of veal quickly sautéed until golden. The dish is traditionally served with a lemon‑caper butter sauce. Veal is pale pink, tender, and has a mild flavor, making scallopini a staple in European cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “scallopini” comes from the Italian “scallopare,” meaning “to thinly slice.”
Veal contains less fat than beef, which makes it a leaner protein option.
Classic scallopini are finished with a butter‑lemon‑caper sauce, sometimes called “mélange.”
In Italy the dish is often paired with pasta, risotto, or a light vegetable side.
Veal scallopini are frequently used in fine‑dining menus as a base for more elaborate sauces.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Veal provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, veal has less saturated fat, supporting heart‑healthy eating patterns.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Mineral source
items.content: Veal contains zinc, iron, and phosphorus, supporting immunity, blood formation, and bone health.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The tender texture of veal makes it easier to digest than tougher cuts of beef.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef or veal.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Although leaner, veal still contains cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne pathogens
items.content: Undercooked veal can harbor bacteria such as Salmonella or E. coli.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions may cause heaviness in those with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve veal scallopini hot, typically drizzled with a lemon‑caper butter sauce. They can be added to salads, tossed with pasta, or used as a sandwich filling. Pair with light sides such as steamed vegetables or a green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw veal pieces in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. Cooked scallopini should be eaten within 24 hours, or stored in a sealed container in the fridge. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Reheat cooked scallopini to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.
